item.title: Another East Jerusalem neighbourhood is demolished, as the UK's diplomats go home
item.description:
Another East Jerusalem neighbourhood is demolished, as the UK's diplomats go home

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Thu, 10/22/2026 - 16:38
Fakhri Abu Diab and his family are among hundreds of people being pushed out of al-Bustan, as Israel takes over residential areas of occupied East Jerusalem
‘We have the right to live peacefully and securely,’ says Fakhri Abu Diab, who is being pushed out of his home in the al-Bustan area of occupied East Jerusalem (Supplied photo)
Off

Down a track and past a pile of debris, 20 or so well-dressed people are waiting, all diplomats. I am joining them on a trip around al-Bustan, a Palestinian neighbourhood in occupied East Jerusalem that has been scheduled for demolition.

Many homes have been destroyed already. Bustan (“the Orchard”) is to be turned into a car park and recreation ground for settlers - but not for Palestinian residents, who will by then be absent.

We stumble past the ruins of what used to be a house. In the garden is a caravan, where we are met by the owner, Fakhri Abu Diab. His wife Ameena, mother of their five children, stands nearby.

“They arrived at three in the morning, armed soldiers with black masks putting a gun to my head,” Fakhri recalls of a recent visit. “They took me to interrogation.”

On another occasion, they broke Ameena’s glasses. Terrified, she “clenched her jaw so hard that she broke her teeth”.

The diplomats shuffle their feet. Fakhri and Ameena, now in their sixties, have lived in Bustan all their lives. Fakhri is chairman of the local residents’ committee, but he won’t be a resident much longer. 

Their temporary home is scheduled for demolition within 21 days of 4 October, when a new demolition order was pasted on his gate. They don’t know where to go next.

“Whenever I hear bulldozers or any machinery, my automatic reaction is that they are coming for us,” Fakhri tells Middle East Eye. 

Reshaping demography

Suitcases stand packed just outside the door. Fakhri explains that bulldozers sometimes arrive without notice, and often leave no time to gather belongings. 

The Jerusalem municipality gives Palestinians the opportunity to “self-demolish”. Fakhri warns that “if you don’t do that, the municipality does it for you and sends you the bill”.

Fakhri says he paid 43,000 shekels ($13,800) when they destroyed his home.

A couple of the diplomats examine their mobile phones. 

'We are not allowed to have an identity or a state. We wish for action, not just words'

- Fakhri Abu Diab

Some 1,500 Palestinians lived in Bustan, located at the bottom of a valley half a mile southwest of Al-Aqsa Mosque. It is being destroyed as part of a massive project to reshape the demography of occupied East Jerusalem. 

According to a statement from the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem, these demolitions are “a clear manifestation of an Israeli policy aimed at engineering the demographic balance and ‘Judaizing’ the neighborhood by exploiting discriminatory laws”. 

The group adds: “These measures are designed to expand Israeli presence and control over one of the most politically and religiously sensitive areas in the region, serving as a crucial component of the broader ethnic cleansing currently unfolding across the West Bank.”

Fakhri, meanwhile, makes a despairing plea to the diplomats: “We ask the world to pressure Israel not to demolish our remaining homes. We have the right to live peacefully and securely in our homes. The international community is allowing Israel to be above international law. Why are you afraid of Israel even when it’s acting against international law?”

He says his house was demolished on Valentine’s Day 2024, one month after Andrew Miller, then the US deputy assistant secretary of state for Israeli-Palestinian affairs, had made an official visit to his home in Bustan.

“Why meet diplomats when our homes get demolished afterwards?” Fakhri asks.

Sleeping in cars

Fakhri says he has also been visited by three delegates from countries that manufacture the bulldozers used to destroy Palestinian houses. “These tools were made to advance civilisation, not to demolish civilisation,” he says. 

Not many diplomats are taking notes. Most are from Europe; some appear bored, but a Swiss delegate seems genuinely interested. 

“What can you do to help?” pleads Fakhri. “We have lost hope. We would like to see help from the international community. We are not allowed to have an identity or a state. We wish for action, not just words.”

He adds a note of warning: “We do not know how the young men will react.”

There are no British diplomats present, Israel having evicted most of them from the British consulate the previous week in reprisal for Britain decision to sanction West Bank settlements.

This change of policy has come too late to rescue Al-Bustan and does not apply here in any case.

It’s the Jerusalem municipality and Israeli government, not Israeli settler terrorism, which is ethnically cleansing Palestinians from East Jerusalem neighbourhoods.

Palestinians are still totally abandoned even after the euphoria of a British shift in policy

The Israeli non-profit organisation Ir Amim shows in a devastating report published yesterday, "Expulsion: The State Architecture of Dispossession", that virtually all Israeli governmental bodies are involved in forcibly displacing East Jerusalemites.

In other words, Palestinians are still totally abandoned even after the euphoria of a British shift in policy.

Fakhri leads us out and past the wreckage of what used to be his home. On our right is a playground, also marked for destruction. On the left is a football pitch. Ditto. 

Everything will be destroyed: property, public amenities, communities, families, lives, hope. 

I ask Fakhri where people will go. “We don’t know. Some are now sleeping in cars.”

We climb some steps into the living room of another house. It belongs to Imad Badran, a 56-year-old blind man, who is challenging his demolition order in court.

“I am disabled,” he says. “I live with my wife who is also disabled, and our son whose house has already been demolished. In my situation, as a blind man, how do I look for a home? Even if there was a place to go, how could I afford the 6-7,000 shekels a month?

“There is no need for these demolitions,” he adds. “If they are carried out, I will be left on the street.” 

Pleas ignored

Badran says he explained all this to a worker from the Jerusalem municipality, who replied: “That’s not my problem.”

One of the diplomats spoke: “It’s important to hear your voice and your words.” 

Israeli settlers 'hike' through my West Bank village. Next is the violent land grab
Read More »

Our next stop was to visit an elderly lady whose house had been demolished last month - but when we arrived, she wasn’t there. It was explained that she’d been waiting for us outside. 

It was the first time she’d been back to her former home, and her son texted Fakhri to say she found it too upsetting, couldn’t bear to speak, and had already left. 

The world’s attention is focused on the wave of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. A few days after our visit, a convoy carrying European diplomats was surrounded and pelted with stones by settlers.

These dispossessions are happening all over occupied East Jerusalem, and are part of the same programme of ethnic cleansing.

Fakhri later told MEE that many famous names have come to Bustan to hear his story: former US President Jimmy Carter, former Irish President Mary Robinson, former US special representative for Palestinian affairs Hady Amr, and the UN undersecretary for humanitarian affairs, Tom Fletcher. Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who was recently awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, has also visited.

All listened and witnessed, to no effect. If the Jerusalem municipality has its way, Bustan - until recently a flourishing Palestinian community - will soon become a car park.

item.title: ‘Hereness’: What the forgotten history of Jewish anti-Zionism can teach us today
item.description:
‘Hereness’: What the forgotten history of Jewish anti-Zionism can teach us today

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Thu, 10/22/2026 - 10:24
As Zionism and Judaism are conflated by supporters of Israel, anti-Zionist Jews are rediscovering a radical Jewish tradition of opposing it
An election poster of the General Jewish Labour Bund reading "Where we live, there is our country!" hung in Kiev, 1917 (Wikimedia Commons)
Off

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out a coalition with the Green Party last week after its members passed a motion declaring that “Zionism is racism”, on the grounds that the party is antisemitic.

The motion argues that Zionism, the ideology behind Israel’s creation, is rooted in colonisation and Jewish ethnic supremacy over Palestinians, positioning the party in opposition to it.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski did not vote on the motion due to certain amendments that failed to pass but describes himself as an anti-Zionist Jew.

He hit back in a post on X, calling Burnham “a Prime Minister who arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it” and accusing him of “the dangerous & irresponsible blurring of challenging Israel & Antisemitism”.

Zionism was a fringe ideology for much of Judaism's modern history, only becoming mainstream in Jewish communities and institutions within the past 75 years.

Nevertheless, defenders of Israel routinely conflate Judaism and Zionism to tar critics of Israel as antisemites, erasing the Jewish identity of anti-Zionists such as Polanski and perpetuating the antisemitic notion that Jewish people are monolithic and singularly invested in the Israeli state.

While most British Jews still identify as Zionists, younger generations are increasingly distancing themselves from the label.

The trend is more pronounced among American Jews - only a third of whom identify as Zionists.

Those aged 18-34 are the most likely to describe themselves as anti-Zionist or non-Zionist. 

Many of these Jews are uncovering a forgotten history of Jewish anti-Zionism and encountering Jewish identities that could once again become a dominant force within the community.

The Bund movement

When Zionism emerged in the 1880s and 90s, it faced opposition from wide sections of Jewish society, particularly among the Bundists.

Founded in Eastern Europe in the late 19th century, the Jewish Labour Bund was a socialist workers’ movement committed to preserving Jewish cultural identity, or Diaspora Nationalism, alongside a broader internationalist class struggle to emancipate workers from capitalism.

By the beginning of the 20th century, it was the largest and best-organised Jewish party in Eastern Europe, claiming 34,000 members across 274 branches.

Molly Crabapple’s recent book, Here Where We Live Is Our Country, traces her family’s Bundist history, and has received widespread acclaim from Jews and non-Jews interested in this past. 

How the UN declared Zionism a form of racism - Britain then lobbied against revoking the resolution
Read More »

“As American Jews turn away from Zionism, they are seeking these … liberatory, solidaristic and universalist histories which are so present in our story,” Crabapple told Middle East Eye.

A central tenet of Bundism, particularly after the Holocaust, was the concept of “hereness” - or “doikayt” in Yiddish - opposing the Zionist notion that Jewish safety depended on an ethnostate halfway across the world. 

“Zionism has always been a movement that gave into antisemitic European logic,” Crabapple continued, submitting to the “European ethnonationalist idea that Jews are foreigners who belong elsewhere”.

Her book documents how Zionists collaborated with Poland’s antisemitic government in the late 1930s, which armed, trained and funded Zionist militias in Palestine and armed youth militias in Poland that murdered Jews.

Arthur Balfour, namesake of the 1917 Balfour Declaration establishing Israel as a “Jewish national home”, described Zionism as a “serious effort to mitigate the age-old miseries created for western civilisation by the presence in its midst of a body [Jewish people] which is too long regarded as alien and even hostile, but which it was equally unable to expel or absorb”.

Edwin Montagu, the only Jewish member of the British Cabinet in 1917, was also the sole member opposing the declaration, predicting that it would “prove a rallying ground for antisemites in every country in the world”. 

For non-Zionist Eastern European Jews facing antisemitism in the 20th century, doikayt articulated “a commitment to worldmaking in the places where Jews lived, called home, [and] belonged for centuries”, explained Miriam Chorley-Schulz, a Holocaust scholar at University of Oregon. 

“Against Zionism’s settler-colonial solution to the ‘Jewish Question’, this commitment opposed Jewish ‘normalisation’ within racial capitalist structures through ethnostate-building in Palestine, insisting on fighting the material and ideological conditions of oppression here and now instead,” she told MEE.

‘Bundist counterculture’

“Opposition to Zionism was as obvious to the Bund as opposing fascism and any other nationalist violence: Jewish nationalism was just as ugly, just as contemptuous as any other,” Eyshe Beirich, who translated an upcoming collection of Yiddish Bundist writings, We, Traitors, told MEE. 

As socialists, Bundists organised Jewish trade unions and mass demonstrations with tens of thousands of Jewish workers and students. 

In Russia, they played a significant role in the revolutions and organised Jewish self-defence during the 1903-1906 pogroms.

Bernard Goldstein, the head of the Bund militia in Poland, advocated for armed resistance to Nazi persecution and helped to smuggle weapons ahead of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto uprising.

'Hyperzionism': How Germany's conflation of antisemitism and anti-Zionism allowed a far-right return
Read More »

Bundists helped establish the first secular Yiddish school system and institutions giving “education, mutual aid, and organisational support to Jewish workers all over Poland”, Beirich said, building what Jack Jacobs called a “Bundist counterculture”.

Yiddish, a European Jewish vernacular spoken by most Jews at the time, was celebrated by the Bund as a secular Jewish language preserving shared culture.

For Bundists, Beirich explained, “Yiddish carried the idioms and revolutionary spirit … of the Jewish working class, and it was incumbent on the Bund to support its development.”

Although some Zionists supported Yiddish education in Poland, most mainstream Zionist parties opposed the school system, and even collaborated with the Polish government to shut them down, Beirich told MEE. 

“The Zionist movement eventually opted for an aggressive Hebrew revivalism - a nationalist monolingual project that deliberately suppressed languages spoken by diasporic Jews … as both a tool of negating the diaspora and nation-building in the settler colony,” Chorley-Schulz added. 

Yiddish, like the Bund itself, was largely destroyed through the Holocaust or assimilation, only surviving in Orthodox or ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities. However, some are now looking to resuscitate both the movement and its language.

The conscious pariah 

Many Jews fleeing Eastern Europe settled in America, bringing “Bundish” ideas which helped build Jewish American socialism during the height of labour organising in the 1880s, joining other immigrants to found mutual aid organisations and celebrate their culture. 

Benjamin Balthauser’s book, Citizens of the Whole World, revisits the history of the American Jewish left. 

Among American Jews, there remains a “long memory of a Jewish fight against fascism, nationalism, racism”, Balthauser explained.

“That was a Bundist idea: that we are proud of our Jewish heritage, of our Jewish identity, but also want to be in solidarity with the working class, with anti-colonial struggles around the world” - including in Palestine.

"There is no need for any one of us to serve in the IDF. The IDF should not exist. The state of Israel should not exist." Former Israeli soldier, Meital Yaniv, talks about her experience in the IDF and how it turned her into a peace activist and an anti-Zionist organiser. https://t.co/Zm3jRPzjZe

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) January 8, 2024

“This memory is coming back … a memory that is buried, but it's a very shallow grave,” Balthauser said, as more American Jews are “remembering this older language, and also realising that this language is not that old”. 

In his new book, Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History, Benjamin Moser explores past and present Jewish anti-Zionists largely overlooked in an effort to elide Judaism with Zionism.

He argued that Jews have traditionally occupied the role Hannah Arendt called the “conscious pariah”, which was part of why they were so often targeted by European elites during times of crisis.

Moser told MEE that what tied together these Jewish anti-Zionists across different places and times was that “they are all pariahs, all resistors” who “don’t want to go along with the rationale of power and violence”.

Arendt, one of the figures he examines, wrote about Zionism as a means of “getting Jews to disengage from their own societies”, rather than see themselves as interconnected with other oppressed people and the wider working class.

Reflecting on Theodor Herzl’s The Jewish State, Arendt wrote in 1946: “Only when we come to see ourselves as part and parcel of a world in which we, like everybody else, are engaged in a struggle against great and sometimes overwhelming odds, and yet with a chance of victory, however small, and with allies, however few… only then will we be able to rid the world of its nightmarish quality.”

For anti-Zionist Jews like Moser, the role for these conscious pariahs is now more important than ever.

item.title: Israel prepares full West Bank lockdown after Hebron shooting
item.description:
Israel prepares full West Bank lockdown after Hebron shooting

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 10:36
Israeli forces shut Hebron’s Ibrahimi Mosque and intensify raids as ministers call to dismantle the Palestinian Authority
Israeli soldier stands guard near a shooting scene in Hebron in the occupied West Bank 23 October 2026 (Reuters/Ammar Awad)
Off

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered preparations for a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank after a shooting in Hebron wounded five Israeli soldiers on Friday.

Two Palestinians opened fire on Israeli troops at a checkpoint in northern Hebron early in the day. 

At least five soldiers were wounded, two of them critically.

The two Palestinians were shot dead after a 20-minute exchange of fire, according to Israeli reports. Israeli media said the men belonged to the same family in Hebron.

Netanyahu said he had held a security assessment following the shooting and ordered Hebron’s closure, alongside preparations for a full lockdown across the West Bank.

The Israeli army said it had placed Hebron “under a cordon” and launched what it called “offensive counterterrorism operations”.

Palestinian media reported Israeli raids in Dura, south of Hebron, during which Israeli forces shot and wounded at least one Palestinian man and arrested others. 

Israeli forces also closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron and expelled its staff and custodians, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Awqaf and Religious Affairs.

The ministry condemned the move as “a flagrant and ongoing violation of the sanctity of Islamic holy sites and freedom of worship, as guaranteed by international conventions and laws”.

Israel trying to 'eliminate' living conditions for Palestinians in occupied West Bank, says report
Read More »

The Ibrahimi Mosque, an endangered Palestinian World Heritage Site recognised by Unesco, has faced mounting Israeli restrictions in recent months. These include barring Muslim worshippers, restricting the call to prayer and facilitating settler incursions.

Israeli army chief Eyal Zamir described Friday’s shooting as “serious” and said troops had “prevented an even more serious attack” by killing the two attackers.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir seized on the incident to renew his call for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority (PA).

“This incident once again illustrates what I have been saying in the Cabinet for four years: this entity known as the Palestinian Authority must be dismantled,” he said on X.

“We must dismantle it and put an end to the shared roads used by Israelis and residents of the Palestinian Authority.

"The freedom of movement of Palestinian Authority residents is less important than our right to live.”

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed the call, demanding a full-scale military campaign across the occupied West Bank.

“There is no alternative to a full-scale military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorist militants. Exactly as in Gaza and Lebanon,” he said, using the biblical names for the West Bank.
